# Workspace README (README.md)

## sindr

[![CI](https://github.com/steffendybvik/sindr-rs/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/steffendybvik/sindr-rs/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/sindr.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/sindr)
[![docs.rs](https://docs.rs/sindr/badge.svg)](https://docs.rs/sindr)
[![License: MIT OR Apache-2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT%2FApache--2.0-blue.svg)](#license)

A circuit simulator you embed in Rust: build a circuit as a typed value, solve it natively or in the browser, and get back numbers checked against ngspice.

### Why sindr

- **Typed in, typed out.** A `Circuit` is a Rust value (or JSON), results are structs, and errors are a `SimError` enum you can match on, not text on stderr.
- **Pure Rust, no C.** No `unsafe` in any crate (each has `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`), no libngspice to install, no global state: run as many simulations in parallel threads as you like.
- **Builds for WebAssembly.** `wasm32-unknown-unknown` with every feature on, so the same engine runs in a web app.
- **Answers design questions.** `check_ratings` says whether each part stays inside its absolute maximum ratings, self-heating flags thermal runaway, and `check_specs` turns `.meas`-style measurements into pass/fail with margins.
- **Real parts as primitives.** 34 element types: the usual R, L, C, sources and semiconductors, plus LEDs, zeners, regulators, op-amps, comparators, relays, fuses, switches, potentiometers, thermistors, photoresistors, transformers, batteries, crystals and ferrite beads.
- **Checked against ngspice.** Every analysis has golden cases solved by both (below).

### Quick start

```toml
[dependencies]
sindr = "0.3"
```

How much current does a red LED draw from 5 V through 220 Ω?

```rust
use sindr::{solve_circuit, Circuit, CircuitElement};
use sindr::element::{Led, Resistor, VoltageSource};

fn main() -> Result<(), sindr::SimError> {
    let circuit = Circuit::new("gnd", vec![
        CircuitElement::VoltageSource(VoltageSource { id: "V1".into(), nodes: ["vcc".into(), "gnd".into()], voltage: 5.0, waveform: None }),
        CircuitElement::Resistor(Resistor { id: "R1".into(), nodes: ["vcc".into(), "a".into()], resistance: 220.0 }),
        CircuitElement::Led(Led { id: "D1".into(), nodes: ["a".into(), "gnd".into()], color: "red".into(), temperature: 300.15 }),
    ]);
    let result = solve_circuit(&circuit)?;
    let led = result.component("D1").expect("D1 is in the circuit");
    println!("{:.1} mA, {:.1} mW", led.current_through * 1e3, led.power * 1e3);
    Ok(())
}
```

More in [`sindr/examples/`](./sindr/examples): RC transient, BJT amplifier, Bode plot, DC sweep, a SPICE deck.

### Crates

| Crate | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| [`sindr`](./sindr) | The simulator and its data model (`Circuit`, elements, waveforms, design hierarchy, part data): operating point, transient, AC, DC and temperature sweeps, `.tf`, `.sens`, `.noise`, `.pz`, loop gain, `.meas`, ratings checks, SPICE front end |
| [`sindr-devices`](./sindr-devices) | Device physics: diode family, BJT, MOSFET, JFET, IGBT, varactor, thermistor and photoresistor models |

`sindr` depends on `sindr-devices`. The split lets you use the device-physics models with your own solver, without the `nalgebra` linear-algebra stack.

Both build for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, with default and all features, so sindr runs in a browser. CI builds them and solves an operating point, an AC sweep, a transient and a SPICE deck under Node on every pull request.

### Accuracy

Each analysis is checked against [ngspice](https://ngspice.sourceforge.io/) 47 on golden circuits solved by both: diodes with their `.model` cards and charge, BJTs, MOSFETs, JFETs, LEDs, controlled sources, transformers, subcircuits. The worst deviation of any quantity at any point, per analysis:

<!-- accuracy:start -->
| Analysis | Cases | Worst relative error | Worst other |
|---|---|---|---|
| Operating point | 22 | 7e-6 | — |
| DC sweep | 8 | 4e-5 | — |
| Temperature sweep | 4 | 8e-7 | — |
| AC | 15 | 3e-6 | 1e-4° phase |
| Diode charge (AC) | 2 | 2e-4 | — |
| Noise | 4 | 7e-7 | — |
| Pole-zero | 2 | 1e-9 | — |
| Transient | 12 | 3e-4 | 2.6 % of full scale |
<!-- accuracy:end -->

The transient's worst is a switching BJT's collector on a 3 µs edge, where a 0.4 mV base error becomes 2.6 % of the current; its other cases stay under 0.15 %. Every case, and the tolerance its test holds it to, is in [`docs/ACCURACY.md`](./docs/ACCURACY.md); how the cases are built is in [`sindr/tests/golden/README.md`](./sindr/tests/golden/README.md). Both tables come from the test suite (`scripts/accuracy_table.py`).

### Speed

Medians on an Apple M1 Pro, release build, one thread ([details](./sindr/README.md#performance)):

| Circuit | Time |
|---|---:|
| Operating point, 100 diodes and resistors | 0.93 ms |
| Transient, 100-stage RC ladder, 200 steps | 15 ms |
| Half-wave rectifier, five 50 Hz cycles (5 000 steps) | 9 ms |

CI fails a pull request that makes any benchmark more than 25 % slower.

#### Against ngspice

The same netlists in both, at their default tolerances, on the same M1 Pro
with ngspice 47 ([`vs_ngspice`](./sindr/examples/vs_ngspice.rs); needs
ngspice, so it isn't in CI). sindr is called in-process. ngspice is either
spawned per run with `ngspice -b`, or driven by one `.control` loop.

| Per call | sindr | ngspice -b |
|---|---:|---:|
| Operating point, BJT stage | 7 µs | 14 ms (all but < 1 ms is startup) |
| AC, series RLC, 61 points | 48 µs | 14 ms (same) |
| Transient, 5 ms of a rectifier | 35 ms | 56 ms (42 ms solving) |

| 1 000 op points, base resistor ±10 % | Time | Op points/s |
|---|---:|---:|
| sindr, 1 thread | 8.8 ms | 114 000 |
| sindr, 4 threads, one process | 3.4 ms | 290 000 |
| ngspice, one process, `.control` loop | 36 ms | 28 000 |
| ngspice -b per point, 10 at once | 2.0 s | 500 |

| Size | sindr | ngspice, solve only |
|---|---:|---:|
| Operating point, 1 000-diode chain | 8.6 ms | 16 ms |
| Operating point, 3 000-diode chain | 27 ms | 82 ms |
| Transient, 1 000-stage RC ladder, 200 steps | 151 ms | 29 ms |
| Transient, 3 000-stage RC ladder, 200 steps | 462 ms | 85 ms |

Embedded, a small solve costs microseconds against ngspice's 14 ms start,
and sindr has no global state, so solves run in parallel threads. ngspice
solves large transients about five times faster: past a few hundred nodes,
a long transient is ngspice's ground ([limits](./LIMITATIONS.md#solver--numerics)).

### When to use sindr

| | sindr | A full SPICE simulator |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | A simulator built to embed, with design checks | A standalone program or C library that runs netlists |
| Main input | `Circuit` values or JSON; a SPICE3 subset (feature `spice`) | SPICE netlists in its own dialect |
| WebAssembly, no C library | Yes | Usually not |
| Ratings, self-heating, pass/fail specs | Built in | Scripted by hand, if at all |
| Analyses | op, DC, AC, transient, temperature, `.tf`, `.sens` (DC and AC), `.noise`, `.pz`, loop gain, `.meas` | Those and more: Fourier, distortion |
| Device models | Shockley diode, Ebers–Moll BJT, MOSFET Level 1, JFET, IGBT, op-amp macromodel, and part-level elements (LED, regulator, relay, battery …) | **Far more:** Gummel–Poon, BSIM, transmission lines, behavioural and code models |
| SPICE dialect coverage | A practical subset | Full |

Use a full SPICE simulator to run existing decks and vendor model libraries as they are. Use sindr to put a simulator inside a Rust program or a web app, describe circuits as data, and ask whether the parts survive.

### SPICE netlist input

A SPICE3 netlist parser ships inside `sindr` as the `spice` feature, on by default like every feature (`default-features = false` and a `features` list keeps only the ones you pick):

```toml
[dependencies]
sindr = "0.3"
```

```rust,ignore
let netlist = sindr::spice::parse_file("amp.cir")?;
let result = sindr::solve_circuit(&netlist.circuit)?;
```

It reads a practical subset of Berkeley SPICE3f5 decks (R, L, C, V, I, D, Q, M, J, B, X, linear E/G/F/H (and `VALUE`, `POLY`), K coupling, `.subckt`, `.global`, `.model`, `.tran`, `.dc`, `.ac`, `.tf`, `.sens`, `.noise`, `.pz`, `.meas`, `.op`, `.ic`, `.nodeset`, `.options`, `.param`, `.include`, `.lib`), keeps `.subckt` hierarchy as blocks and instances (flattened with `.`-separated naming when simulated), and returns a `SourceMap` to recover original instance paths. `to_netlist` writes a `Circuit` back out, `.subckt`s included. See the [`sindr::spice`](https://docs.rs/sindr/latest/sindr/spice/) module docs for the exact supported subset and strictness options.

`sindr::spice::to_netlist` goes the other way: it writes a `Circuit` as a SPICE deck (R, L, C, V, I with waveforms, D and Q with `.model` cards, E/G/F/H, transformers as L–L–K, and exact R/D equivalents for switches, fuses, potentiometers, LEDs and the like) that ngspice runs, and that `parse_str` reads back. Elements with no SPICE equivalent are an `ExportError`.

A runnable walkthrough (parse → solve → dispatch directives → render a diagnostic) lives in [`sindr/examples/parse_netlist.rs`](./sindr/examples/parse_netlist.rs):

```bash
cargo run --example parse_netlist
```

### Status

`0.3.0`, [published on crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/sindr). Until 1.0, a breaking change bumps the minor version (`0.4.0`) and anything else the patch (`0.3.1`), so `sindr = "0.3"` never breaks on `cargo update`. The road to 1.0 is in [`ROADMAP.md`](./ROADMAP.md).

### Scope & limitations

sindr is an analog circuit simulator. Digital logic, HDL ingestion, MCU simulation, schematic capture, vendor model cards, pole-zero analysis, BSIM-class device models, and coupled thermal networks (beyond one thermal RC per part) are **not** supported today. SPICE netlist import is available as a parser for a practical subset (see above), not full SPICE3 coverage. See [`LIMITATIONS.md`](./LIMITATIONS.md) for the full breakdown of what's out-of-scope versus not-yet-implemented.

Where it's heading on the way to 1.0 is in [`ROADMAP.md`](./ROADMAP.md). To work on sindr itself, see [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](./CONTRIBUTING.md). AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, etc.) should also read [`AGENTS.md`](./AGENTS.md) for layout, conventions, and pitfalls.

# Crate `sindr` README (sindr/README.md)

## sindr

MNA (Modified Nodal Analysis) circuit solver. Build a circuit, call `solve_circuit`, get voltages, currents, and power for every component.

Supports: resistive DC, nonlinear DC (Newton-Raphson), transient (Gear-2, trapezoidal or backward Euler), AC analysis, noise (`.noise`), transfer function (`.tf`), DC and AC sensitivity (`.sens`), pole-zero (`.pz`), loop gain with stability margins, DC sweep, and temperature sweep. The solver picks the right path automatically based on what components are in the circuit.

Device physics (BJT, MOSFET, diode models) live in the companion crate [`sindr-devices`](../sindr-devices).

### Add to your project

```toml
[dependencies]
sindr = "0.3"
```

Every feature is on by default: `serde`, `schemars` (JSON Schema), `spice` (netlist parsing and export), `examples` (the named example circuits) and `parallel` (Monte Carlo and corners across threads, serial on wasm). To keep only some, turn the defaults off and list them:

```toml
sindr = { version = "0.3", default-features = false, features = ["serde", "spice"] }
```

Parsing a SPICE netlist:

```rust,ignore
let netlist = sindr::spice::parse_file("amp.cir")?;
let result = sindr::solve_circuit(&netlist.circuit)?;
```

It reads a practical subset of Berkeley SPICE3f5 decks (R, L, C, V, I, D, Q, M, J, B, X, linear E/G/F/H (and `VALUE`, `POLY`), K coupling, `.subckt`, `.global`, `.model`, `.tran`, `.dc`, `.ac`, `.tf`, `.sens`, `.noise`, `.pz`, `.meas`, `.op`, `.ic`, `.nodeset`, `.options`, `.param`, `.include`, `.lib`), keeping `.subckt` hierarchy as blocks and instances, which are flattened with `.`-separated naming when simulated. See the `sindr::spice` module docs for the supported subset and strictness options, or run the worked example:

```bash
cargo run --example parse_netlist
```

`sindr::spice::to_netlist` goes the other way: it writes a `Circuit` as a SPICE deck (R, L, C, V, I with waveforms, D and Q with `.model` cards, E/G/F/H, transformers as L–L–K, and exact R/D equivalents for switches, fuses, potentiometers, LEDs and the like) that ngspice runs, and that `parse_str` reads back. Elements with no SPICE equivalent are an `ExportError`.

### Quick start

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
use sindr::{Circuit, CircuitElement, solve_circuit};
use sindr::element::{Resistor, VoltageSource};

let circuit = Circuit {
    ground_node: "gnd".into(),
    components: vec![
        CircuitElement::VoltageSource(VoltageSource {
            id: "V1".into(),
            nodes: ["n1".into(), "gnd".into()],
            voltage: 10.0,
            waveform: None,
        }),
        CircuitElement::Resistor(Resistor {
            id: "R1".into(),
            nodes: ["n1".into(), "n2".into()],
            resistance: 1_000.0,
        }),
        CircuitElement::Resistor(Resistor {
            id: "R2".into(),
            nodes: ["n2".into(), "gnd".into()],
            resistance: 2_000.0,
        }),
    ],
    ..Default::default()
};

let result = solve_circuit(&circuit)?;

println!("n2 = {:.3} V", result.voltage("n2").unwrap());           // 6.667 V
println!("R1 current = {:.3} mA", result.current("R1").unwrap() * 1e3); // 3.333 mA
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

### Building circuits

Every component has an `id` (arbitrary string) and `nodes` (node names as strings). One node must match `ground_node` — it is held at 0 V.

#### Passive components

```rust,ignore
use sindr::element::{Capacitor, Inductor, Resistor};
CircuitElement::Resistor(Resistor { id, nodes: [String; 2], resistance: f64 })
CircuitElement::Capacitor(Capacitor { id, nodes: [String; 2], capacitance: f64 })
CircuitElement::Inductor(Inductor { id, nodes: [String; 2], inductance: f64, saturation: Option<InductorSaturation> })
```

Capacitors and inductors trigger transient analysis automatically. In pure DC (no reactive elements, no waveforms), they are treated as open circuits.

An inductor with `saturation: Some(InductorSaturation { i_sat, l_sat })` has a core that saturates: its flux is `λ(i) = l_sat·i + (inductance − l_sat)·i_sat·tanh(i/i_sat)`, so its inductance falls from `inductance` at zero current towards `l_sat` past `i_sat` (to 42 % of the way at `i_sat`, 7 % at `2·i_sat`). A datasheet's saturation current, where L has dropped 20–30 %, is about `0.6·i_sat`. The transient integrates the flux, and AC and noise use the incremental inductance `dλ/di` at the DC current. There's no hysteresis or core loss; add a resistor for loss.

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
# use sindr::element::Inductor;
use sindr_devices::inductor::InductorSaturation;

// 10 µH that saturates around 3 A, keeping 1 µH when saturated.
let l1 = CircuitElement::Inductor(Inductor {
    id: "L1".into(),
    nodes: ["sw".into(), "out".into()],
    inductance: 10e-6,
    saturation: Some(InductorSaturation { i_sat: 3.0 / 0.6, l_sat: 1e-6 }),
});
```

#### Sources

```rust,ignore
use sindr::element::{CurrentSource, VoltageSource};
CircuitElement::VoltageSource(VoltageSource { id, nodes: [String; 2], voltage: f64, waveform: Option<Waveform> })
CircuitElement::CurrentSource(CurrentSource { id, nodes: [String; 2], current: f64, waveform: Option<Waveform> })
```

`nodes[0]` is the positive terminal for voltage sources. A current source's current flows through it from `nodes[0]` to `nodes[1]`: it is drawn out of `nodes[0]` and pushed into `nodes[1]`, as SPICE's `I` does.

A `Waveform` (sine, pulse, square, triangle, PWM, PWL) on any source triggers transient analysis. See [`waveform.rs`](src/waveform.rs) for the `Waveform` enum.

#### Battery

```rust,ignore
use sindr::element::Battery;
CircuitElement::Battery(Battery { id, nodes: [String; 2], params: BatteryParams, state_of_charge: f64 })
```

`nodes` are `[positive, negative]`. The cell is an equivalent circuit: open-circuit voltage by state of charge (`params.ocv`, interpolated), behind a series resistance `r_series` and an optional RC pair (`params.rc`) for the slow sag after a load step and the recovery after it. Its terminal voltage is `OCV(SoC) − R0·i − v1`.

- **DC:** the open-circuit voltage at `state_of_charge` behind `R0 + R1`.
- **Transient:** the RC pair charges, and the state of charge falls by the charge drawn, `dSoC/dt = −i/(3600·capacity)`. Each step's `state_of_charge` (and the result's, at the end) holds it by battery id. Below 0 the cell is over-discharged and holds its 0 % voltage. A battery with an RC pair makes `solve_circuit` run a transient.
- **AC:** the impedance `R0 + R1‖C1`.

`current_through` flows `nodes[0] → nodes[1]` inside the cell, as for a voltage source, so it is negative while discharging. Presets: `BatteryParams::lithium_ion(capacity_ah, r_series)` (a typical Li-ion/LiPo rest curve, 3.27–4.20 V), `BatteryParams::cr2032()` (a 225 mAh coin cell with its pulse-recovery pair) and `BatteryParams::constant(volts, capacity_ah, r_series)`.

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
use sindr::battery::BatteryParams;
use sindr::element::Battery;

// A 500 mAh LiPo at 80 %, 0.15 Ω.
let cell = CircuitElement::Battery(Battery {
    id: "B1".into(),
    nodes: ["vbat".into(), "0".into()],
    params: BatteryParams::lithium_ion(0.5, 0.15),
    state_of_charge: 0.8,
});
```

#### Switches

```rust,ignore
use sindr::element::{Pushbutton, Switch};
CircuitElement::Switch(Switch { id, nodes: [String; 2], closed: bool })
CircuitElement::Pushbutton(Pushbutton { id, nodes: [String; 2], closed: bool })
```

Modeled as a 0.01 Ω resistor when closed, 1 GΩ when open.

```rust,ignore
use sindr::element::SwitchSpdt;
CircuitElement::SwitchSpdt(SwitchSpdt { id, nodes: [String; 3], position: SpdtPosition })  // [common, a, b]
```

A single-pole double-throw switch: common to `a` (`SpdtPosition::A`, the default) or to `b`, each path a `Switch`. Its result is the path in use: common minus the selected throw, and the current from common into it.

#### Crystal and ferrite bead

```rust,ignore
use sindr::element::{Crystal, FerriteBead};
CircuitElement::Crystal(Crystal { id, nodes: [String; 2], params: CrystalParams })
CircuitElement::FerriteBead(FerriteBead { id, nodes: [String; 2], params: FerriteBeadParams })
```

- **Crystal:** the Butterworth–Van Dyke model, `Rm`–`Lm`–`Cm` in series beside `C0`, with `Lm` set by the series-resonant `frequency`. `CrystalParams::from_datasheet(frequency, esr, c0)` takes `Cm = C0/250`, typical of AT-cut crystals; set `cm` when you know it. Open at DC. Its result's `power` is what `Rm` dissipates, the drive level, which `Ratings::power` limits. The load capacitance a datasheet names is the two capacitors on your board, not part of the crystal.
- **Ferrite bead:** `r_dc` in series with `l ∥ r_ac` (∥ `c`, when set). `FerriteBeadParams::from_datasheet(z_100mhz, r_dc)` fits `l` and `r_ac` to the impedance at 100 MHz; fit all four to the curve when the peak matters. `Ratings::current` is its rated current.

Both, and the SPDT switch, are solved as those networks: results and ratings come back under the element's own id, and `to_netlist` writes the network.

#### Diodes

```rust,ignore
use sindr::element::{Diode, Led, Photodiode, SchottkyDiode, ZenerDiode};
CircuitElement::Diode(Diode { id, nodes: [String; 2], model: Option<DiodeModel> }) // silicon (Vf ≈ 0.7 V) unless a SPICE-style model is set
CircuitElement::Led(Led { id, nodes: [String; 2], color: String }) // "red"|"orange"|"amber"|"yellow"|"green"|"blue"|"white", any case
CircuitElement::ZenerDiode(ZenerDiode { id, nodes: [String; 2], vz: f64 })   // breakdown voltage at 5 mA
CircuitElement::SchottkyDiode(SchottkyDiode { id, nodes: [String; 2] })            // Vf ≈ 0.3 V
CircuitElement::Photodiode(Photodiode { id, nodes: [String; 2], irradiance: f64 }) // irradiance in W
```

All diodes use Newton-Raphson automatically when present. `Diode`'s optional `model` is what a SPICE `.model D` card fills in: `DiodeModel { is, n, rs }` (defaults `1e-14`, `1`, `0`), the junction charge `cjo`, `vj`, `m`, `fc`, `tt` (defaults `0`, `1`, `0.5`, `0.5`, `0`) and breakdown `bv`, `ibv` (defaults none, 1 mA). With `cjo` or `tt` set the diode stores charge, so it shows reverse recovery in transient and a capacitance in AC, and the circuit takes the transient path; its `current_through` then includes the charging current, while `power` stays the dissipation. `bv` adds SPICE's exponential reverse breakdown, fitted to pass `ibv` near `−bv` as ngspice does. A `ZenerDiode` is exactly such a diode: `bv = vz`, `ibv` = 5 mA (a small zener's test current) and `rs` = 1 Ω, so it matches ngspice with the card `D(IS=1e-14 N=1 RS=1 BV=vz IBV=5m)`. Each diode variant accepts an optional `temperature: f64` field (K, default 300.15 K): IS scales with the SPICE temperature formula and the thermal voltage is kT/q at that temperature.

#### Varactor diode

```rust,ignore
use sindr::element::Varactor;
CircuitElement::Varactor(Varactor {
    id: String,
    nodes: [String; 2],  // [anode, cathode]
    params: VaractorParams, // { cj0, phi, m }
})
```

Varactors are purely reactive — treated as open circuit in DC, as their junction capacitance at the bias point in AC, and stamped as a voltage-dependent capacitor `C_j(V) = cj0 / (1 - V/phi)^m` each transient timestep. Always triggers transient analysis.

#### Transistors

```rust,ignore
use sindr::element::{Bjt, Igbt, Jfet, Mosfet};
// BJT — nodes: [base, collector, emitter]
CircuitElement::Bjt(Bjt {
    id,
    nodes: [String; 3],
    kind: BjtKind,                          // BjtKind::Npn or BjtKind::Pnp
    bf: f64,                                // forward beta, default 100
    temperature: f64,                       // junction temp (K), default 300.15 K
    parasitic_caps: Option<BjtParasiticCaps>, // { cbe, cbc } in Farads; None = disabled
    model: Option<BjtModel>,                // IS, BR, NF, NR, VAF; None = built-in defaults
})

// MOSFET — nodes: [gate, drain, source]; body tied to source
CircuitElement::Mosfet(Mosfet {
    id,
    nodes: [String; 3],
    kind: MosfetKind,                          // MosfetKind::Nmos or MosfetKind::Pmos
    params: MosfetParams,                      // KP, VTO, LAMBDA, GAMMA, PHI; VTO SPICE-signed (negative for PMOS)
    parasitic_caps: Option<MosfetParasiticCaps>, // { cgs, cgd } in Farads; None = disabled
    body_diode: Option<DiodeModel>,            // power MOSFET's body diode; None = none
})

// IGBT — nodes: [gate, collector, emitter]
CircuitElement::Igbt(Igbt {
    id,
    nodes: [String; 3],
    params: IgbtParams, // { vth, k, vce_sat }
})

// JFET — nodes: [gate, drain, source]
CircuitElement::Jfet(Jfet {
    id,
    nodes: [String; 3],
    kind: JfetKind, // JfetKind::NChannel or JfetKind::PChannel
    idss: f64,      // drain saturation current at Vgs = 0 (A)
    vp: f64,        // pinch-off voltage (V), negative for N-channel
    parasitic_caps: Option<JfetParasiticCaps>, // { cgs, cgd, pb, m, fc } gate junctions; None = disabled
})
```

A JFET's `parasitic_caps` are SPICE's gate junctions: CGS and CGD at zero bias, each `C0/(1 − v/PB)^M` at its junction voltage and continued linearly above `FC·PB`, with SPICE's defaults `PB = 1`, `M = 0.5`, `FC = 0.5`. Transient integrates their charge; AC and noise take the capacitance at the bias point.

A MOSFET's `body_diode` is a SPICE diode card (`DiodeModel`) from source to drain for NMOS, drain to source for PMOS. It conducts when a bridge or inductive load pulls the drain past the source with the channel off. Every analysis solves it as a `Diode` named `<id>.body`, which is where its current shows in the results; `bv` on it sets the part's avalanche voltage.

`BjtKind`, `MosfetKind`, `JfetKind`, `IgbtParams` and `VaractorParams` are re-exported from `sindr` directly. `BjtParasiticCaps`, `MosfetParasiticCaps` and `JfetParasiticCaps` live in `sindr::circuit`, and `MosfetParams` in `sindr_devices::mosfet`.

When `parasitic_caps` is set, Cbe/Cbc (BJT) or Cgs/Cgd (MOSFET) are stamped as capacitor companions each transient timestep, with per-junction voltage state tracked internally, and as jωC in AC; a JFET's CGS/CGD as charge companions, with per-junction charge state. This automatically triggers transient analysis.

**NPN common-emitter example:**

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
use sindr::{Circuit, CircuitElement, BjtKind, solve_circuit};
use sindr::element::{Bjt, Resistor, VoltageSource};

let circuit = Circuit {
    ground_node: "0".into(),
    components: vec![
        CircuitElement::VoltageSource(VoltageSource {
            id: "Vcc".into(), nodes: ["vcc".into(), "0".into()], voltage: 10.0, waveform: None,
        }),
        CircuitElement::Resistor(Resistor {
            id: "Rc".into(), nodes: ["vcc".into(), "collector".into()], resistance: 1_000.0,
        }),
        CircuitElement::Resistor(Resistor {
            id: "Rb".into(), nodes: ["vcc".into(), "base".into()], resistance: 470_000.0,
        }),
        CircuitElement::Bjt(Bjt {
            id: "Q1".into(),
            nodes: ["base".into(), "collector".into(), "0".into()],
            kind: BjtKind::Npn,
            bf: 100.0,
            temperature: 300.15,
            parasitic_caps: None,
            model: None,
        }),
    ],
    ..Default::default()
};

let result = solve_circuit(&circuit)?;

let q1 = result.bjt("Q1").unwrap();
println!("Vbe = {:.3} V, Vce = {:.3} V, Ic = {:.3} mA, region = {}",
    q1.vbe, q1.vce, q1.ic * 1000.0, q1.region);
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

#### Transformer (coupled inductors)

```rust,ignore
use sindr::element::Transformer;
CircuitElement::Transformer(Transformer {
    id: String,
    nodes: [String; 4],  // [p1, q1, p2, q2] — primary (p1,q1), secondary (p2,q2)
    l1: f64,             // primary inductance (H)
    l2: f64,             // secondary inductance (H)
    k: f64,              // coupling coefficient [0, 0.999]; default 0.999 (near-ideal)
})
```

Mutual inductance M = k·√(L1·L2). In DC analysis both windings are short circuits. In AC and transient, two branch current unknowns (one per winding) are added to the MNA system, so the windings are coupled through M. k=1 is mathematically singular — use k≤0.999.

#### Controlled sources

```rust,ignore
use sindr::element::{Behavioural, Cccs, Ccvs, Vccs, Vcvs};
// Voltage-controlled voltage source: V_out = gain × V_ctrl
CircuitElement::Vcvs(Vcvs { id, nodes: [out+, out-], control_nodes: [ctrl+, ctrl-], gain: f64 })

// Voltage-controlled current source: I_out = gm × V_ctrl
CircuitElement::Vccs(Vccs { id, nodes: [out_from, out_to], control_nodes: [ctrl+, ctrl-], gm: f64 })

// Current-controlled voltage source: V_out = rm × I_ctrl
CircuitElement::Ccvs(Ccvs { id, nodes: [out+, out-], control_source: String, rm: f64 })

// Current-controlled current source: I_out = alpha × I_ctrl
CircuitElement::Cccs(Cccs { id, nodes: [out_from, out_to], control_source: String, alpha: f64 })

// Behavioural source (SPICE's B): a voltage or current set by an expression
CircuitElement::Behavioural(Behavioural { id, nodes: [n+, n-], output: BehaviouralOutput, expr: Expression })
```

A behavioural source's `expr` is `Expression::parse("v(a)*v(b)")?` and the like: `v(n)`, `v(n,m)`, `i(source)` (the branch current of a voltage source, VCVS, CCVS, op-amp, regulator or behavioural voltage source), `time`, arithmetic, comparisons, `c ? a : b` and ngspice's functions (`exp`, `tanh`, `limit`, `min`, `u`, …). `BehaviouralOutput::Voltage` holds `V(n+) − V(n-)` at the expression; `Current` drives it from `n+` to `n-`. Newton gets the exact Jacobian by automatic differentiation; AC linearises at the bias point. In JSON the expression is its text: `{"type": "behavioural", "output": "voltage", "expr": "v(a)*v(b)", …}`.

`control_source` is the `id` of the voltage source whose branch current is sensed, positive from its `+` terminal through it to `-`, as in SPICE.

The current sources follow SPICE's `G` and `F` and sindr's own `CurrentSource`: a positive `I_out` flows through the source from `out_from` to `out_to`, so it is drawn out of `out_from` and pushed into `out_to`.

#### Op-amp / Comparator

```rust,ignore
use sindr::element::{Comparator, OpAmp};
// nodes: [in_plus, in_minus, out]
CircuitElement::OpAmp(OpAmp { id, nodes: [String; 3], v_pos: f64, v_neg: f64, model: Option<OpAmpModel> }) // rails, default ±15 V
CircuitElement::Comparator(Comparator { id, nodes: [String; 3], v_pos: f64, v_neg: f64 }) // output high / low, default ±15 V
```

With `model: None` the op-amp is a high-gain VCVS (gain 1×10⁵) with no frequency response, and the rails aren't enforced. A comparator has the same gain and no frequency response, but its output is clamped to `v_neg`/`v_pos`, so overdrive beyond `v_pos / 1e5` (50 µV for a 5 V rail) pins it to a rail in DC, transient and AC (where its gain at a rail is zero). It has no hysteresis or open-collector output; `v_pos` must be above `v_neg`. An `OpAmpModel` turns the op-amp into a macromodel. It has open-loop `gain` (default 1e5), a dominant pole from `gbw` (default 1 MHz), a `slew_rate` limit (default 0.5 V/µs), `r_out`, `offset_voltage` and `bias_current`, and its output clamps to `v_pos`/`v_neg` with anti-windup. A non-inverting stage of gain G then has its −3 dB point near `gbw / G`, and a large step rises at the slew rate:

```rust
use sindr::{CircuitElement, OpAmpModel};
use sindr::element::OpAmp;

let u1 = CircuitElement::OpAmp(OpAmp {
    id: "U1".into(),
    nodes: ["in".into(), "fb".into(), "out".into()],
    v_pos: 12.0,
    v_neg: -12.0,
    model: Some(OpAmpModel { gbw: Some(3e6), slew_rate: Some(13e6), r_out: 50.0, ..OpAmpModel::default() }),
});
```

The pole and slew limit act in transient and AC runs. An op-amp doesn't count as reactive, so `solve_circuit` still runs DC for a circuit whose only dynamics are op-amps; call `solve_transient` to see them.

#### Sensors / misc

```rust,ignore
use sindr::element::{Fuse, Photoresistor, Potentiometer, Relay, Thermistor, VoltageRegulator};
CircuitElement::Photoresistor(Photoresistor { id, nodes: [String; 2], light_level: f64 }) // 0.0 (dark, ~1 MΩ) – 1.0 (bright, ~1 kΩ)
CircuitElement::Thermistor(Thermistor { id, nodes: [String; 2], temperature: f64 }) // Kelvin, default 298.15 K (25 °C)
CircuitElement::Potentiometer(Potentiometer { id, nodes: [top, wiper, bottom], resistance: f64, position: f64 }) // position 0.0–1.0
CircuitElement::Relay(Relay {
    id,
    nodes: [String; 4],     // [coil+, coil-, contact1, contact2]
    coil_resistance: f64,
    pickup_voltage: f64,
    inductance: f64,        // coil inductance (H); 0.0 = purely resistive (default)
})
CircuitElement::Fuse(Fuse { id, nodes: [String; 2], rating: f64, blown: bool }) // 1 mΩ intact, 1 GΩ blown; rating is display-only
CircuitElement::VoltageRegulator(VoltageRegulator { id, nodes: [input, output, gnd], voltage: f64, model: Option<RegulatorParams> })
```

When `inductance > 0`, the relay coil is modeled as an RL circuit in transient analysis (L stamped as an inductor companion). This triggers transient automatically.

`VoltageRegulator` is a linear regulator. With headroom it holds `voltage` above its ground pin (a negative `voltage` is a negative regulator such as a 7905: the same characteristic mirrored, with the input below ground and the output current flowing in at the output pin); without it the output follows the input down by the dropout; past the current limit it holds the current, short circuits included. It draws its output current plus its quiescent current from the input. `model: None` is ideal (no dropout, no quiescent current, no limit) but still never puts out more than it gets in. `RegulatorParams` sets `dropout` (V, plus `dropout_resistance` Ω for one that grows with load), `quiescent_current`, `current_limit`, `line_regulation` (V/V) and `output_resistance` (Ω, load regulation). `RegulatorParams::lm7805()` and `RegulatorParams::ams1117()` are datasheet presets. Its result is the pass element: `voltage_across` is `Vin − Vout`, `current_through` the output current, and `power` the dissipation `(Vin − Vout)·Iout + Vin·Iq`, which the ratings checks and self-heating use. In AC, input ripple reaches the output through line regulation (all of it in dropout). Foldback and thermal shutdown are not modelled.

### Hierarchy and part data

A `Block` is a reusable definition, what `.subckt` is in SPICE. An `Instance` places one and binds its ports to the caller's nets. Inside a block a net is a port, ground, a global (`Circuit::globals`) or local to each instance. `Circuit::flatten` expands it all, naming elements and local nets with the instance path (`X1.R1`, `X1.mid`). Every analysis flattens for you.

```rust,ignore
use sindr::{Block, Circuit, CircuitElement, Instance, Part};
use sindr::element::{Resistor, VoltageSource};

let r = |id: &str, a: &str, b: &str| CircuitElement::Resistor(Resistor {
    id: id.into(),
    nodes: [a.into(), b.into()],
    resistance: 1e3,
});

let mut circuit = Circuit::new(
    "0",
    vec![CircuitElement::VoltageSource(VoltageSource {
        id: "V1".into(),
        nodes: ["in".into(), "0".into()],
        voltage: 10.0,
        waveform: None,
    })],
);
circuit.blocks.insert(
    "divider".into(),
    Block {
        ports: vec!["top".into(), "out".into()],
        components: vec![r("R1", "top", "out"), r("R2", "out", "0")],
        ..Block::default()
    },
);
circuit.instances.push(Instance::new("X1", "divider", ["in", "mid"]));
circuit.parts.insert(
    "V1".into(),
    Part { symbol: Some("Simulation_SPICE:VDC".into()), ..Part::default() },
);

let flat = circuit.flatten().unwrap();
let ids: Vec<&str> = flat.components.iter().map(|c| c.id()).collect();
assert_eq!(ids, ["V1", "X1.R1", "X1.R2"]);
```

`Part` data is ignored by the simulator, except `Part::ratings`: absolute maximum `Ratings` that `check_ratings` compares a simulation against. Empty hierarchy and part fields are left out of JSON, so a flat circuit serialises exactly as before.

### Reading results

`solve_circuit` returns `Result<SimulationResult, SimError>`. Read it by name:

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
# let circuit = Circuit::default();
let result = solve_circuit(&circuit)?;

let vout = result.voltage("out");            // Option<f64>; ground reads Some(0.0)
let i_r1 = result.current("R1");             // its current_through, A
let r1 = result.component("R1");             // Option<&ComponentResult>: V, I, P
let i_v1 = result.branch_current("V1");      // MNA branch current, negative when sourcing
let q1 = result.bjt("Q1");                   // also mosfet(..), op_amp(..), relay(..)

// Inside a block instance or a SPICE subcircuit, by instance path.
let v_sw = result.instance("X1").instance("X2").voltage("sw"); // node X1.X2.sw
let i_l = result.instance("X1.X2").current("L1");               // component X1.X2.L1
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

Every accessor returns `None` for a name the result doesn't have. Names are exact: a parsed SPICE deck's are lowercase (`instance("x1")`). Inside an instance only its own nets and components get the path; a port is the net it's bound to outside, and ground and globals keep their names, so read those on the parent. `InstanceResult::name("sw")` gives the flat name (`"X1.X2.sw"`) for the AC, sweep and transient accessors below.

| Result | By name |
|--------|---------|
| `TimestepSnapshot` | `voltage(node)`, `current(id)`, `component(id)` |
| `TransientData` | `node_voltage_curve(node)` and `component_current_curve(id)` as `(t, value)`; `voltage_at(node, t)`, `current_at(id, t)`, interpolated |
| `AcPoint` | `voltage(node)` (complex), `magnitude(node)`, `phase_deg(node)`, `gain_db(node, ref)` |
| `AcResult` | `node_voltage_curve(node)` (complex), `magnitude_curve`, `gain_curve` (dB), `phase_curve` (°) as `(Hz, value)` |
| `DcSweepResult`, `TempSweepResult` | `node_voltage_curve(node)`, `component_current_curve(id)` as `(sweep value, value)`; each point's `result` has the accessors above |

The fields behind them stay public:

```rust,ignore
pub struct SimulationResult {
    pub node_voltages:    HashMap<String, f64>,  // every node including ground (0.0)
    pub branch_currents:  HashMap<String, f64>,  // voltage source branch currents by id
    pub component_results: Vec<ComponentResult>, // V, I, P for every component
    pub bjt_results:      Vec<BjtResult>,        // present only if circuit has BJTs
    pub mosfet_results:   Vec<MosfetResult>,     // present only if circuit has MOSFETs
    pub op_amp_results:   Vec<OpAmpResult>,      // present only if circuit has op-amps
    pub relay_results:    Vec<RelayResult>,      // present only if circuit has relays
    pub transient:        Option<TransientData>, // present only for reactive/waveform circuits
}

pub struct ComponentResult {
    pub id:              String,
    pub voltage_across:  f64,
    pub current_through: f64,
    pub power:           f64,
}

pub struct BjtResult {
    pub id: String, pub vbe: f64, pub vce: f64,
    pub ib: f64, pub ic: f64, pub ie: f64,
    pub power: f64, pub region: BjtRegion, // Active | Saturation | Cutoff
}

pub struct MosfetResult {
    pub id: String, pub vgs: f64, pub vds: f64,
    pub id_current: f64, pub power: f64, pub region: MosfetRegion, // Cutoff | Triode | Saturation
}
```

For transient circuits, `result.transient` contains a time series. `solve_circuit` picks the duration (5 τ) and step (τ/50) from the circuit's time constants; to set them yourself, as SPICE's `.tran tstep tstop` does, use `solve_transient`:

```rust,ignore
use sindr::{solve_transient, TransientConfig};

// 10 ms in 1 µs steps; optionally cap the step with .with_tmax(…)
let result = solve_transient(&circuit, &TransientConfig::new(10e-3, 1e-6))?;
```

Each snapshot is the end of one step, with sources evaluated at that time; the last is at `tstop`. The default integrator is Gear-2 (second order, no ringing); `.with_method(IntegrationMethod::Trapezoidal)` keeps an LC tank's amplitude exactly, and `IntegrationMethod::BackwardEuler` matches sindr before 0.1.0-alpha.7. Every method takes its first step as backward Euler.

A run starts switched on at t = 0 by default: capacitors uncharged and inductors at 0 A, unless `.with_initial_voltages(…)` or `.with_initial_current(…)` say otherwise (SPICE's `.ic` with `UIC`), so power-on inrush shows. `.with_start(TransientStart::OperatingPoint)` starts from the DC operating point instead, as SPICE's `.tran` without `UIC` does: each source at its t = 0 value, capacitors charged and inductors and transformer windings carrying its currents, with any initial voltages and currents held while it's solved. A SPICE deck's `ParsedNetlist::transient_config()` sets the run up the way ngspice does: the start, `.ic`, `tmax`, and `tstart` (`.with_tstart(t)`: integrate from 0, keep the steps from `t` on).

Steps are at most `tstep` long and every multiple of `tstep` gets a snapshot. In between, the stepper shortens steps where the local truncation error would exceed SPICE's default tolerances, and lands exactly on each corner of a source waveform (pulse edges, PWL points, square-wave flips), so a 1 ns edge in a 1 ms run is resolved without 1 ns steps everywhere. `result.transient.stats` counts accepted and rejected steps; `.with_fixed_step()` turns the error control off.


```rust,ignore
pub struct TransientData {
    pub timesteps: Vec<TimestepSnapshot>,
    pub time_step: f64,
    pub duration:  f64,
}

pub struct TimestepSnapshot {
    pub time:              f64,
    pub node_voltages:     HashMap<String, f64>,
    pub component_results: Vec<ComponentResult>,
}
```

#### CSV export

`TransientData`, `AcResult`, `DcSweepResult` and `TempSweepResult` each have `to_csv()`. It writes one row per point: the scale first (`time`, `frequency`, the swept source's id, or `temperature` in K), then `v(<node>)` for each node in name order, then `i(<id>)` (each component's `current_through`) in circuit order. AC writes each node as `re(v(<node>))` and `im(v(<node>))`. Numbers read back as the same `f64`, and names with commas or quotes are quoted.

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
# let result = solve_circuit(&Circuit::default())?;
std::fs::write("rc.csv", result.transient.unwrap().to_csv())?;
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

#### Progress and cancel

`solve_transient_with_progress` calls a hook after every accepted step with the time reached, the fraction done, and the step's snapshot, so a caller can show a long run's progress and its waveforms as they grow. Returning `Flow::Stop` ends the run with `SimError::Cancelled`. The hook runs on the solving thread; in a browser, solve in a web worker and stop when the page's cancel flag is set.

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
# let circuit = Circuit::default();
let result = solve_transient_with_progress(&circuit, &TransientConfig::new(1.0, 1e-4), |p| {
    if p.accepted_steps % 1000 == 0 {
        println!("{:.0}%", 100.0 * p.fraction());
    }
    Flow::Continue
});
```

#### Transient sessions

`solve_transient` runs to `tstop` in one call. A `TransientSession` holds the run open, for a circuit paired with something outside it: firmware on an emulated microcontroller, a user turning a knob, a sensor whose surroundings change. It follows FMI 3.0 co-simulation: `advance_to(t)` integrates to `t` (FMI's `doStep`), `set_source(id, value)` and `set_param(id, Param::…)` change an input at the time reached, and `run_until(t_max, &[Event])` stops early at the first event, located to its tolerance.

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
# let circuit = Circuit::default();
let mut sim = TransientSession::new(&circuit, &TransientConfig::new(10.0, 100e-6))?;
sim.keep_steps(false); // read voltages, don't build up 10 s of snapshots
for k in 1..=10_000 {
    sim.advance_to(k as f64 * 1e-3)?;                 // one firmware tick
    let adc = sim.voltage("adc0").unwrap();
    sim.set_source("D13", if adc > 2.5 { 5.0 } else { 0.0 })?;
}
let hit = sim.run_until(10.0, &[Event::crosses("int0", 2.5, Edge::Rising)])?;
# Ok::<(), SimError>(())
```

- **A change is a breakpoint.** The step that reached the time saw the old value, the next sees the new, and the integration restarts there with a short backward-Euler step, as at a waveform's corner. Writing a value a source already has changes nothing.
- **What can change:** a voltage or current source's value (a waveform it had is dropped), and with `Param` a resistance, a potentiometer's wiper, a switch, pushbutton or SPDT throw, a photoresistor's light level, a photodiode's irradiance, and the temperature of a thermistor or a junction device that isn't self-heated.
- **Events** are a node crossing a level (`Edge::Rising`, `Falling`, `Either`). The session steps back and re-steps until the crossing is inside the event's tolerance (`Event::within`, default 10⁻⁴ of `tstep`), and stops just after it with the node past the level. Steps tried and undone along the way aren't kept.
- **State survives between calls:** the flat circuit, node map, matrix layout and histories are set up once. Each step still assembles and factors its matrix.
- **Results stream:** `drain_steps()` takes the steps kept since the last call; `voltage(node)` reads the solution directly, and `current(id)` and `last_step()` the latest step. `advance_to_with_progress` takes the same hook as `solve_transient_with_progress`, and a cancelled session carries on from where it stopped. No threads are needed, so it runs as is in `wasm32`.
- The session ends at the config's `tstop` and records from its `tstart`. After an error other than `Cancelled` it refuses to go on.

#### Which engine produced a result

`sindr::VERSION` (and `sindr::devices::VERSION`) is the crate's version as a string, such as `"0.3.0"`. Store it with saved results, so a rerun can tell a change in the design from a change in the engine.

### AC analysis

Small-signal frequency response around the DC operating point. Nonlinear devices are linearised at the operating point, then each frequency is a complex MNA solve.

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
# let mut circuit = Circuit::default();
use sindr::ac_analysis::{solve_ac, AcConfig, FrequencySpacing};

// 51 points from 1 Hz to 100 kHz, driving V1 (the voltage source that
// carries the AC stimulus) with 1 V at 0°.
let config = AcConfig::new("V1", 1.0, 100_000.0, 51)
    .with_spacing(FrequencySpacing::Logarithmic); // the default; or Linear
let result = solve_ac(&circuit, &config)?;

let gain = result.gain_curve("n_out");   // (Hz, dB)
let phase = result.phase_curve("n_out"); // (Hz, degrees)
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

`num_points` counts both endpoints; with 1, only `f_start` is solved. Invalid configs (0 points, non-finite values, `f_start > f_stop`, `f_start <= 0` with logarithmic spacing) return `SimError::InvalidComponent`.

### Transfer function

SPICE's `.tf`: the small-signal DC gain from an input source to an output, the resistance the input source sees, and the output resistance, all at the DC operating point (capacitors open, inductors shorted, nonlinear devices linearised).

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
# let mut circuit = Circuit::default();
use sindr::{solve_tf, TfConfig, TfOutput};

// Output V(out), or TfOutput::current("Vsense"); input a voltage or current source.
let config = TfConfig::new(TfOutput::voltage("out"), "V1");
let tf = solve_tf(&circuit, &config)?;
println!("{} V/V, Rin {} Ω, Rout {} Ω", tf.gain, tf.input_resistance, tf.output_resistance);
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

The input resistance is infinite when the input source draws no small-signal current. Every other independent source is zeroed for the output resistance. A current output (`I(Vx)`) runs from the source's `nodes[0]` through it to `nodes[1]`, as SPICE's.

### Sensitivity

SPICE's `.sens`: the derivative of one DC output with respect to each component parameter, at the operating point. One adjoint solve covers them all, however many there are.

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
# let mut circuit = Circuit::default();
use sindr::{solve_sensitivity, SensConfig, TfOutput};

let config = SensConfig::new(TfOutput::voltage("out")); // or TfOutput::current("Vsense")
let sens = solve_sensitivity(&circuit, &config)?;

for e in &sens.entries {
    println!("{}: {} per unit, {} per +1 %", e.component_id, e.sensitivity, e.per_percent);
}
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

Entries cover resistance, voltage and current source values, the gains of all four controlled sources (VCVS, VCCS, CCVS, CCCS), and device-model parameters: a diode's IS, N and RS, a BJT's BF, IS, BR, NF, NR and VAF, and a MOSFET's KP, VTO and LAMBDA. A device has an entry per parameter; `sens.get_parameter("D1", SensParameter::SaturationCurrent)` picks one. Each is the total derivative, the operating point moving with the parameter. Capacitors, inductors and the other devices (LED, Zener, Schottky, photodiode, JFET, IGBT) get no entry.

`.sens v(out) ac dec 10 1 1meg` is the AC form: at each frequency, the derivative of the output phasor with respect to R, C, L, the controlled-source gains, the stimulus's AC magnitude and the same device parameters, plus a diode's CJO and TT. One adjoint solve per frequency. As in ngspice, the DC operating point is held fixed: a device parameter's entry is its effect on that device's small-signal conductances and capacitances, not through a shift of the bias, so a source's DC value has no AC entry.

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
# let circuit = Circuit::default();
use sindr::ac_analysis::AcConfig;
use sindr::{solve_ac_sensitivity, AcSensConfig, SensParameter, TfOutput};

let config = AcSensConfig::new(TfOutput::voltage("out"), AcConfig::new("V1", 10.0, 1e6, 51));
let sens = solve_ac_sensitivity(&circuit, &config)?;
for (f, s) in sens.curve("C1", SensParameter::Capacitance) {
    println!("{f} Hz: dV(out)/dC1 = {s}");
}
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

For a deck, `ParsedNetlist::ac_sens_config()` builds the `AcSensConfig` from the `.sens ... ac` card and the `AC` spec on the source line.

### Noise

SPICE's `.noise`: thermal noise of resistances and FET channels, shot noise of junction currents, and flicker (1/f) noise where a model sets `KF`, at an output voltage and referred back to an input source. One adjoint solve per frequency gives every source's share.

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
# let mut circuit = Circuit::default();
use sindr::{solve_noise, NoiseConfig};

// V(out) referred to V1, 41 log-spaced points from 10 Hz to 100 kHz.
let noise = solve_noise(&circuit, &NoiseConfig::new("out", "V1", 10.0, 100e3, 41))?;

println!("{:.2} µV rms at the output", noise.total_output_noise * 1e6);
for (source, total) in noise.sources.iter().zip(&noise.source_totals) {
    println!("  {} ({:?}): {:.2} µV", source.component, source.kind, total * 1e6);
}
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

Each point has the output and input-referred densities (`output_density()`, `input_density()`, per √Hz) and each source's contribution. The totals integrate over the band as ngspice does. Noise is at 27 °C. Sources, controlled sources, op-amps, comparators, regulators and a diode's series resistance are noiseless.

### Pole-zero

SPICE's `.pz`: the poles and zeros of the transfer function from an input node pair to an output node pair, at the DC operating point. A voltage gain's poles are those of the circuit with the input shorted (by the voltage source already across it, or one the analysis adds); a transimpedance drives a current into the input pair, left open.

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
# let mut circuit = Circuit::default();
use sindr::{solve_pz, PzConfig, PzFind};

// SPICE `.pz in 0 out 0 vol pz`; PzConfig::transimpedance for `cur`.
let pz = solve_pz(&circuit, &PzConfig::voltage_gain("in", "0", "out", "0"))?;
for p in &pz.poles {
    println!("pole {:.4e} {:+.4e}j rad/s", p.re, p.im);
}
println!("stable: {}", pz.is_stable());
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

Roots are in rad/s, finite ones only, sorted by magnitude. They are the generalised eigenvalues of the linearised `G + sC` pencil (and of its bordered form for the zeros): sindr deflates the infinite ones exactly, by orthogonal reductions, then runs QZ, so a well-separated root is accurate to about 1e-12 relative and a repeated one to about √ε. `with_find(PzFind::Poles)` or `PzFind::Zeros` skips the other half. A transimpedance into a pair a voltage source shorts has no response, and is an error.

### Loop gain and stability margins

The loop gain of a feedback loop at a break point, by Tian's double injection: a voltage and a current injected at a probe, a 0 V voltage source in series with the loop with its `nodes[1]` on the driving side (the amplifier output) and `nodes[0]` on the driven side (the feedback network). The loop isn't cut, so both sides keep their loading, and the result is exact for loops that pass signal both ways through the probe.

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
# let mut circuit = Circuit::default();
use sindr::{solve_loop_gain, LoopGainConfig};

// Vprobe: nodes ["fb_in", "out"], 0 V. 801 log-spaced points, 1 Hz to 100 MHz.
let lg = solve_loop_gain(&circuit, &LoopGainConfig::new("Vprobe", 1.0, 100e6, 801))?;
println!("crossover {:?} Hz", lg.gain_crossovers);
println!("phase margin {:?}°, gain margin {:?} dB", lg.phase_margin_deg, lg.gain_margin_db);
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

`T` is the return ratio, positive at low frequency for negative feedback. Each point has `gain` (complex), `gain_db()` and the phase unwrapped along the sweep, so the sweep must be dense enough that the phase moves less than 180° between points. Crossovers are refined by bisection on `T` itself, so the margins don't depend on the grid. The phase margin is the smallest over every 0 dB crossing, the gain margin the smallest over every −180° crossing; each is `None` when there is no crossing in the sweep.

### DC sweep

Sweep a voltage or current source across a range and collect operating points at each step. Each point's Newton–Raphson starts from the one before, as in SPICE.

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
# let mut circuit = Circuit::default();
use sindr::{Circuit, CircuitElement, dc_sweep};

let sweep = dc_sweep(&circuit, &DcSweepAxis::new("V1", 0.0, 5.0, 51))?;

let v_curve = sweep.node_voltage_curve("n2");
let i_curve = sweep.component_current_curve("D1");
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

Two sources, one inside the other (SPICE's `.dc VDS 0 5 0.1 VGS 0 3 0.5`), draw a family of device curves: one `DcSweepResult` along the inner source per value of the outer one.

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
# let mut circuit = Circuit::default();
use sindr::{dc_sweep_nested, dc_sweep::DcSweepAxis};

let family = dc_sweep_nested(
    &circuit,
    &DcSweepAxis::from_step("VDS", 0.0, 5.0, 0.1)?, // inner, fastest
    &DcSweepAxis::from_step("VGS", 0.0, 3.0, 0.5)?, // outer
)?;
for curve in &family.curves {
    let id_vs_vds = curve.sweep.component_current_curve("M1");
    println!("VGS = {} V: {} points", curve.outer_value, id_vs_vds.len());
}
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

A parsed `.dc` card gives its axes with `analysis.dc_axes()`.

### Temperature sweep

Solve a circuit at a series of junction temperatures and collect operating points. Useful for BJT Ic vs. temperature curves and thermal characterisation.

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
# let mut circuit = Circuit::default();
use sindr::{Circuit, temperature_sweep, TempSweepResult};

// All junction devices (BJT, diode, LED, Zener, Schottky, Photodiode) have their
// temperature field overridden at each step.
let result = temperature_sweep(&circuit, &TempSweepConfig::new(250.0, 350.0, 11))?; // 250 K → 350 K, 11 points

for point in &result.points {
    let ic = point.result.bjt("Q1").map_or(0.0, |b| b.ic);
    println!("T = {:.1} K, Ic = {:.3} mA", point.temperature, ic * 1000.0);
}
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

```rust,ignore
pub struct TempSweepResult {
    pub start:  f64,                 // K
    pub stop:   f64,                 // K
    pub points: Vec<TempSweepPoint>,
}

pub struct TempSweepPoint {
    pub temperature: f64,              // K
    pub result:      SimulationResult, // the full operating point at this temperature
}
```

`num_points` must be ≥ 2, and both temperatures finite and above 0 K.

### Self-heating

Give a part a thermal path and the solver heats its junction by what it dissipates, then feeds that temperature back into the device: IS and kT/q for diodes, LEDs, Zeners, Schottkys, photodiodes and BJTs, and the resistance of a thermistor. The DC solve iterates until power and temperature agree. A transient carries a thermal RC state per part (`Cθ·dT/dt = P − (T − ambient)/Rθ`), starting cold at ambient.

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
# let mut circuit = Circuit::default();
use sindr::{solve_circuit, Part, SimError, Thermal};

// SOT-23 on its own (~500 K/W), or a TO-220 on a heatsink.
circuit.parts.insert("Q2".into(), Part { thermal: Some(Thermal::junction_to_ambient(500.0)), ..Part::default() });
circuit.parts.insert("Q3".into(), Part { thermal: Some(Thermal::on_heatsink(5.0, 10.0)), ..Part::default() });

match solve_circuit(&circuit) {
    Ok(result) => println!("Tj(Q2) = {:.1} K", result.junction_temperatures["Q2"]),
    Err(SimError::ThermalRunaway { part, temperature }) => println!("{part} runs away past {temperature:.0} K"),
    Err(e) => return Err(e),
}
# Ok::<(), SimError>(())
```

`Thermal` takes `rth_ja` (K/W), or `rth_jc` plus `rth_ca` for a part on a heatsink, an optional `cth` (J/K; without it a transient's junction follows its power with no lag), and `ambient` (K, default 300.15). With it, the element's own `temperature` field is ignored. `SimulationResult::junction_temperatures` and each `TimestepSnapshot`'s carry the result, and `Ratings::tj_max` is checked against them. When no balance exists (a junction past 1000 K, or the iteration never settles), the solve returns `SimError::ThermalRunaway`. AC, `.tf`, `.sens` and `.noise` solve the same heated bias point and linearise each device at its junction temperature. MOSFETs, JFETs, IGBTs and resistors report a junction temperature, but their models don't depend on it.

### Monte Carlo and corners

`sindr::variation` repeats any analysis with parts varied within their tolerances and takes your `Measurement`s on every run:

```rust,ignore
use sindr::variation::{corners, monte_carlo, Corners, MonteCarloConfig, Parameter, Tolerance};

// Every resistor ±1 % (Gaussian, the band at 3σ), and C1 ±10 % uniform.
let mut tolerances = Tolerance::on_every(&circuit, Parameter::Resistance, 0.01);
tolerances.push(Tolerance::uniform("c1", Parameter::Capacitance, 0.10));

let mc = monte_carlo(&circuit, &MonteCarloConfig::new(tolerances.clone(), 1000).with_seed(1),
                     &[bandwidth], |c| solve_ac(c, &ac))?;
let s = mc.stats("f3db").unwrap();          // mean, std_dev, min, max, measured, failed
let yield_ = mc.yield_within("f3db", 1.4e3, 1.8e3);

let worst = corners(&circuit, &tolerances, &Corners::All, &[bandwidth], |c| solve_ac(c, &ac))?;
```

Worst case on top of the runs: `mc.check_specs(&specs)` gives each spec's pass, fail and unmeasured counts, its yield, and the `WorstRun` nearest or furthest past a limit (with its signed margin and the tolerance values behind it). `ratings_over(&circuit, &Sampling::Corners { tolerances, which: Corners::All }, solve_op)` runs `check_ratings` on every run and reports each part and rating at its worst: value, margin, the run, its tolerance values, the time for a transient, and how many runs exceeded it.

A `Tolerance` varies one component's resistance, capacitance, inductance or source value by a relative band, uniformly or Gaussian (`sigmas` standard deviations across the band, 3 by default). `corners` runs every low/high combination (up to 16 tolerances) or a `Corners::List`. Each run draws from its own seeded stream, so a seed repeats exactly, and the `parallel` feature spreads runs across threads without changing them. A run whose analysis fails is kept with its error, and counted in `failed`.

### Ratings checks

Check a solved circuit against each part's absolute maximum ratings, so nothing gets powered past its datasheet limits. Ratings live on the component's `Part` (`circuit.parts`, keyed by component id). `check_ratings` looks at the DC operating point, or at every step of a transient, where inrush, inductive kickback and start-up peaks show up.

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
# let mut circuit = Circuit::default();
use sindr::{check_ratings, solve_transient, Part, Ratings, RatingStatus, TransientConfig};

circuit.parts.insert("Q1".into(), Part {
    ratings: Ratings { vce: Some(45.0), ic: Some(0.1), power: Some(0.5), ..Ratings::default() },
    ..Part::default()
});

let result = solve_transient(&circuit, &TransientConfig::new(1e-3, 1e-6))?;
let report = check_ratings(&circuit, &result)?;
for c in report.exceeded() {
    println!("{} {:?}: {:.3} {} at t = {:?} (limit {:?}, margin {:.0}%)",
        c.part, c.rating, c.worst.unwrap(), c.rating.unit(), c.time, c.limit,
        c.margin_percent.unwrap_or(f64::NAN));
}
assert!(report.is_safe()); // false while anything is exceeded *or* unverified
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

Each component kind has ratings it needs, checked whether set or not; a missing one is `RatingStatus::Unverified`, never a pass:

| Component | Needs |
|---|---|
| resistor, potentiometer, thermistor, photoresistor | `power` |
| capacitor | `voltage` |
| inductor | `current` |
| diode, Schottky, LED, photodiode | `reverse_voltage`, `forward_current`, `power` |
| Zener | `power` |
| varactor | `reverse_voltage` |
| BJT | `vce`, `vcb`, `veb`, `ic`, `power` |
| MOSFET, JFET | `vds`, `vgs`, `id`, `power` |
| IGBT | `vce`, `vgs` (gate–emitter), `ic`, `power` |
| anything with `Part::thermal` | also `tj_max` |

Any other rating set on a part is checked too: `power`, `voltage` and `current` on any component (on the port its `ComponentResult` reports), the rest on the devices they belong to. All limits are magnitudes, so PNP and PMOS parts use the same positive numbers. Transistor power is `|V·I|` on the Vce/Ic or Vds/Id port, without base or gate dissipation.

### Measurements and specs

Turn a result into numbers, and the numbers into a verdict. A `Measurement` reads a `Signal` (`v(out)`, `v(a, b)`, `i(R1)`, in dB or phase on AC) off any result: a transient, AC, DC or temperature sweep, or an operating point. A `Spec` adds limits, and `check_specs` reports each one's value, limits, pass/fail and margin.

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
# let mut circuit = Circuit::default();
use sindr::measure::{check_specs, Crossing, Measure, Measurement, Signal, Spec, Stat};

let tran = solve_transient(&circuit, &TransientConfig::new(10e-3, 1e-6))?;
let specs = [
    Spec::new(Measurement::new("vout", Measure::stat(Signal::v("out"), Stat::Avg)).window(5e-3, 10e-3))
        .between(4.9, 5.1),
    Spec::new(Measurement::new("ripple", Measure::stat(Signal::v("out"), Stat::PeakToPeak)).window(5e-3, 10e-3))
        .at_most(0.05),
    Spec::new(Measurement::new("settle", Measure::settling(Signal::v("out"), 0.05))).at_most(2e-3),
];
let report = check_specs(&tran, &specs).with_ratings(check_ratings(&circuit, &tran)?);
for c in report.failed() {
    println!("{}: {:?} outside {:?}..{:?} by {:?}", c.name, c.value, c.min, c.max, c.margin);
}
assert!(report.passed()); // every spec passed and every part is within its ratings
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

| `Measure` | SPICE `.meas` | Gives |
|---|---|---|
| `Find { at }` | `FIND v(out) AT=1m` | value at x, interpolated |
| `Stat` | `AVG`, `RMS`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `PP`, `INTEG` (and `Final`) | statistic over the window (`FROM=`/`TO=`) |
| `When(Crossing)` | `WHEN v(out)=2.5 RISE=2` | x of the nth rising, falling or any crossing, or the last |
| `Delay { trig, targ }` | `TRIG … VAL= … TARG … VAL=` | x(targ) − x(trig) |
| `Transition` | | rise or fall time between fractions of the swing (10–90 %) |
| `Settling { band }` | | time from the window start until it stays within ±band of its final value |
| `Bandwidth { drop_db }` | `WHEN vdb(out)=-3 FALL=1` | first x after the peak `drop_db` below it (−3 dB point) |

A measurement that can't be taken (an unknown node, a level never crossed, a phase on a transient) is `SpecStatus::Unmeasured` with a reason, never a pass; `Measurement::on` returns it as `SimError::Measurement`. Average and RMS are weighted by step width, so the transient's uneven steps don't skew them. With the `spice` feature, `.meas tran|ac|dc` cards land in `ParsedNetlist::measurements`, each with the analysis it measures.

### Fourier analysis and FFT

`sindr::fourier` takes the spectrum of a transient signal. `Fourier` is SPICE's `.four`: the harmonics of the last period at a fundamental, each with its magnitude and phase, and the THD, computed as ngspice computes them (a 200-point linear resample of the last period). `Fft` resamples a span onto a power of two of points, applies a window and returns one-sided bins scaled to peak amplitude, so a bin-centred sine reads its own amplitude.

```rust,no_run
# use sindr::*;
# let circuit = Circuit::default();
use sindr::fourier::{Fft, Fourier, Window};
use sindr::measure::Signal;

let result = solve_transient(&circuit, &TransientConfig::new(5e-3, 5e-6))?;
let four = Fourier::new(1e3).on(&result, &Signal::v("out"))?;
println!("THD {:.2} %, 3rd harmonic {:.3} V", four.thd_percent, four.harmonic(3).unwrap().magnitude);

let spectrum = Fft::new().window(Window::Hann).span(1e-3, 5e-3).on(&result, &Signal::v("out"))?;
for bin in spectrum.bins.iter().filter(|b| b.magnitude > 1e-3) {
    println!("{:>8.0} Hz  {:.4} V", bin.frequency, bin.magnitude);
}
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

The run should have settled by the span analysed: a start-up transient leaks into every bin. `Fourier::of` and `Fft::of` take a `(time, value)` trace you already have. A bin-centred tone stays within `Window::half_width` bins of its own (0 for rectangular, 1 for Hann and Hamming, 2 for Blackman, 4 for flat-top); see the module docs for the windows' coefficients.

### Importing a schematic netlist

`sindr::import` is for editors: map your netlist onto it and simulate a schematic without writing a SPICE deck. A `Netlist` holds components (your id, a `ComponentKind`, a value as a number or text, named parameters, an optional model and `Part`) and nets (your id, an optional display name, and the `(component, terminal)` pins on it). A `Bench` adds what the schematic leaves out: the ground net, sources and loads attached to nets or terminals (a connector pin, a test point), nets to tie together (an analog ground to ground), and the analysis to run.

```rust
use sindr::import::{simulate, Analysis, Bench, BenchSource, Component, ComponentKind, Net, Netlist, Simulation};

let netlist = Netlist {
    components: vec![
        Component::new("c1", ComponentKind::Resistor).with_value("10k"),
        Component::new("c2", ComponentKind::Resistor).with_value("4k7"),
    ],
    nets: vec![
        Net::new("vin", [("c1", "1")]),
        Net::new("vout", [("c1", "2"), ("c2", "1")]),
        Net::new("gnd", [("c2", "2")]),
    ],
};
let bench = Bench::new("gnd")
    .with_source(BenchSource::voltage("supply", "vin", 5.0))
    .with_analysis(Analysis::OperatingPoint);
let Simulation::OperatingPoint(op) = simulate(&netlist, &bench).unwrap().result else { unreachable!() };
println!("vout = {:.3} V", op.voltage("vout").unwrap());
```

- **Ids carry through.** Element ids are your component ids and node names your net ids, so results land on your parts. Every `ImportError` names the component, net or bench item: an unknown kind, a terminal the kind doesn't have, a terminal on two nets or on none, a value that isn't one.
- **Terminals by name, never pin number:** `anode`/`cathode` (or `A`/`K`), `B`/`C`/`E`, `G`/`D`/`S`, `in+`/`in-`/`out` (or `Non-inverting`, `Inverting`, `Output`, `Positive supply`, `Negative supply`), case ignored and `-`, `_` and spaces alike. Unpolarised two-terminal parts also take `1` and `2`. `ComponentKind::terminals` lists each kind's names. A MOSFET's `body` must sit on its source's net; an op-amp's `V+`/`V-` pins set its rails from the bench supplies on those nets.
- **Netlists as an editor exports them.** `ComponentKind::from_name` reads symbol ids (`resistor-iec`, `capacitor-polarized`, `op-amp`, `push-button`, `switch-spst`, `test-point`, `header-4`). When nets name terminals by id and the names sit in a table on each component, pass the table with `ImportOptions::with_terminal_names` to `Netlist::to_circuit_with` or `import::simulate_with`: a named terminal matches by its name, an unnamed one by its id, so pin `1` of an LED still needs its `Anode` name.
- **Dual and quad op-amps and comparators.** `dual_op_amp`, `quad_op_amp`, `dual_comparator` and `quad_comparator` (or `op-amp-dual` and the like) are one package whose units share its `V+`/`V-` pins. Each unit becomes its own element, `<id>.a`, `<id>.b` …, with terminals tagged by unit as datasheets write them: `1IN+`, `IN1-`, `INA+`, `-IN B`, `OUT A`, `2OUT`. A spare unit with nothing connected adds no element.
- **Black boxes for what sindr can't simulate.** A `ComponentKind::BlackBox` (an IC) adds no element, but its terminals stay bench attach points. Unknown kinds are refused by default; `ImportOptions::with_unknown_kinds(UnknownKinds::BlackBox)` keeps them as black boxes instead. Every black box is listed in `ImportedCircuit::black_boxes` with the nets it's on, so none is skipped silently. A net a black box leaves with one element or no DC path to ground (a capacitor or a MOSFET's gate isn't one), such as a pull-up into an MCU input or a resistor between two IC pins, is tied to ground through 1 TΩ (`HIGH_IMPEDANCE_OHMS`, an input's leakage and SPICE's gmin) so the rest solves, and listed in `ImportedCircuit::high_impedance`.
- **Vendor subcircuits as models** (feature `spice`). `Model::Subckt(SubcktModel::new(text, name, pins))` simulates a part with a vendor's `.subckt`: the text as shipped, which subcircuit, and the part's terminal for each of its ports. The part becomes an instance under its own id (internal nodes `U1.…`), parse warnings come back as import warnings, and a bad pin map is an error naming the pin.
- **Schematics still being drawn.** A required terminal on no net refuses the import by default. `ImportOptions::with_unconnected(UnconnectedTerminals::Skip)` leaves that component out instead (its connected nets stay), warns about it, and lists it in `ImportedCircuit::skipped`; open ends (a net only one element reaches, parts not yet wired to ground) get the 1 TΩ tie. The finished part of a design simulates. An editor's "exclude from simulation" attribute maps onto `ComponentKind::BlackBox`.
- **Values as schematics write them**, through `import::parse_value`: `4k7`, `4R7`, `2M2`, `100nF`, `4.7 µF`, `10 kΩ`, `300 K`. Case matters as on a schematic, so `1M` is a megohm (SPICE would read a milliohm).
- **Connectors, test points, net ties and mounting holes** add no element; a bench attaches to their terminals. Crystals (`16MHz`, with `esr` and `c0`) and ferrite beads (`600` Ω at 100 MHz, with `r_dc`) import as their equivalent circuits.
- **Bench loads** are resistors, capacitors and inductors, plus `LoadKind::CurrentSink` (a constant current drawn from `a` into `b`, such as an IC's supply current; for one that changes with time, use a current `BenchSource` with a waveform) and `LoadKind::TimedSwitch`, which is closed through `on_resistance` until `at` and then open at `off_resistance`, or open then closed with `starts_closed: false`. `LoadKind::released_at(1e-6, 25.0)` is an open-drain output holding a bus line low and letting go at 1 µs, for its rise time through the pull-ups and bus capacitance. The operating point, DC sweeps and AC see it at t = 0; a transient lands a step on `at`, which still sees the old state, as a waveform's jump does.
- **Power ports are only names.** A net called `3V3` isn't driven unless the bench says so. `Bench::with_supplies_from_net_names` adds a supply for every net whose name states a voltage (`3V3`, `+5V`, `-12V`), on request only. Decorated names (`3V3_A`, `12V_IN`) get none, since they're often rails derived through a filter or a switch. A net the bench already drives, or ties to one it drives, gets no second supply, and tied nets get one between them. `import::supply_names` reports what that assumes, which supply-like names (`VCC`, `VBAT`, `3V3_A`) were left for you to set, and which nets are named like grounds.
- Everything is serde, so a netlist and bench can come in as JSON. The `ComponentKind` docs list each kind's value, parameters and model.

#### What sindr reads from part data

An editor's parts library knows more about a part than its value: a datasheet's forward voltage, gain, threshold. Export those as parameters and sindr fits its models to them; leave them out and sindr uses its default model for the kind, and says so.

| Kind | Reads | Fitted |
|---|---|---|
| `led` | `color`/`colour` (`red`, `orange`, `amber`, `yellow`, `green`, `blue`, `white`, any case), or a colour word in the value (`Amber`, `LED red 3mm`) | the colour's preset (≈ 1.8–3.2 V at 20 mA) |
| `led` | `vf` (V) at `if` (A), optionally `vf2` at `if2` | a diode through that point (N = 2), with Vf falling 2 mV/K |
| `diode` | `vf` (V) at `if` (A), optionally `vf2` at `if2` | IS (N = 1), or IS and N through both points |
| `zener_diode` | `vz` (V) or the value, at `iz` (A) | breakdown so that it carries `iz` at `vz` |
| `npn`, `pnp` | `hfe` (ratio) at `hfe_ic` (A); `vce_sat` (V) at `vce_sat_ic` and `vce_sat_ib` (A) | `bf` = hFE; BR through Vce(sat) |
| `nmos`, `pmos` | `vth` (V) at `vth_id` (A); `rds_on` (Ω) at `rds_on_vgs` (V), optionally at `rds_on_id` (A) | Level-1 KP and VTO through both |

- **Min, typ and max.** Each figure (`vf`, `vf2`, `vz`, `hfe`, `vce_sat`, `vth`, `rds_on`) also takes `_min`, `_typ` and `_max` (`hfe_min`, `vce_sat_max`). A fit uses the typical value, else the middle of min and max, else whichever is given. Test conditions (`if`, `iz`, `vth_id` …) are exact.
- **Units an editor's library has.** Numbers are in base units (V, A, Ω, a plain ratio), as numbers, text (`"20 mA"`, `"0.2 V"`) or typed quantities: `Value::Quantity` holds the number, its `Unit` (`Ohm`, `F`, `H`, `V`, `A`, `W`, `Hz`, `s`, `m`, `K`, `1`) and the text shown, `{"value": 0.02, "unit": "A", "text": "20 mA"}` in JSON. A quantity in the wrong unit for its parameter is an error.
- **Nothing falls back silently.** `ImportedCircuit::models` records each component's `ModelSource` (model, value, params, datasheet or default), and `ImportedCircuit::warnings` has a warning for every component that got the default: a transistor whose value is only a part number (`PMBT3904`, bf = 100), an LED with no colour (red), a diode with no `vf`. Warnings don't stop the import.
- **Spaces don't merge.** `parse_value` keeps a number and a unit apart when a space is between them: `"300 K"` is 300 kelvin and `"0.01 1"` the ratio 0.01, while `300K` is still 300 k as a schematic writes it.
- The constructors are public: `DiodeModel::from_datasheet`, `DiodeModel::led_from_datasheet`, `DiodeModel::zener_from_datasheet`, `BjtModel::from_datasheet` and `MosfetParams::from_datasheet`, with the figures in `sindr::datasheet`.

### Examples

One small program per capability in [`examples/`](./examples), run with `cargo run -p sindr --example <name>`:

| Example | Shows |
|---|---|
| `voltage_divider` | Linear DC operating point |
| `bjt_amplifier` | Nonlinear DC with a BJT |
| `transient_rc` | Transient step response |
| `bode_plot` | AC analysis |
| `transfer_function` | Transfer function (`.tf`) |
| `sensitivity` | DC sensitivity (`.sens`) |
| `dc_sweep_diode` | DC sweep (diode I–V curve) |
| `temperature_sweep` | Temperature sweep |
| `initial_voltages` | Seeding Newton–Raphson (`.nodeset`) |
| `import_netlist` | Importing a schematic netlist with a test bench |
| `parse_netlist` | SPICE input |
| `list_examples`, `run_example` | The built-in named circuits |

### Error handling

```rust,ignore
pub enum SimError {
    Design(DesignError),
    NoGround,
    DisconnectedNodes(Vec<String>),
    FloatingNode(String),
    SingularMatrix,
    InvalidSolution,
    InvalidComponent(String),
    InvalidResistance(String),
    ConvergenceFailed {
        iterations: usize,
        max_step_volts: f64,
        node: Option<String>,
        components: Vec<String>,
        at: SolvePoint,
    },
    ThermalRunaway { part: String, temperature: f64 },
    Measurement { name: String, reason: String },
}
```

`ConvergenceFailed` means Newton-Raphson did not converge — usually caused by a nonlinear circuit with no DC path to ground, or component values far outside typical operating ranges. The `max_step_volts` field gives the largest per-node Newton step (V) on the final iteration, useful for distinguishing slow convergence from genuine divergence. `node` is the node that took it, `components` the parts on that node, and `at` where the analysis failed (`SolvePoint::OperatingPoint`, `DcSweep`, `Temperature` or `Transient { time }`), so the message points at the part to fix. (Note: this is a step magnitude `max_i |V_new[i] − V_prev[i]|`, not a KCL residual `|F(x)|`.)

`ThermalRunaway` means self-heating found no thermal balance (`temperature` is the junction's, in K, when the solve gave up), `Measurement` that a measurement couldn't be taken on a result, and `Design` that the block hierarchy can't be flattened.

### Solver routing

`solve_circuit` picks a path automatically — you never select it manually:

| Circuit contains | Solver used |
|---|---|
| Only linear elements | Direct MNA (LU factorisation) |
| Nonlinear elements (diodes, BJTs, MOSFETs, IGBTs, comparators…) | Newton-Raphson iteration |
| Reactive elements (C, L, Varactor, Transformer, parasitic caps, a diode whose model sets `cjo` or `tt`) or waveform sources | Transient (Gear-2 by default) |
| Both reactive and nonlinear | Transient with per-step Newton-Raphson |

The transient solver steps up to `tstep` (or `tmax`, if smaller), shortens a step where the local truncation error would exceed SPICE's default tolerances (RELTOL 1e-3, VNTOL 1 µV, TRTOL 7), and lands exactly on every corner of a source waveform. A step whose Newton-Raphson solve fails is halved and retried. One that fails even at a millionth of `tstep` is a regenerative edge with nothing to slow it (a multivibrator's or Schmitt trigger's, transistors without junction capacitance): the node voltages jump while the capacitors hold theirs, and the stepper follows the jump by pseudo-transient continuation, then restarts the integration after it. `stats.jumped_steps` counts those.

### Performance

Medians from `cargo bench -p sindr --bench transient --bench newton` on an Apple M1 Pro (release build, one thread). The circuits are in `sindr/benches/`.

| Case | 10 | 100 | 1 000 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| DC, diode–resistor chain (devices) | 37 µs | 0.93 ms | 8.7 ms |
| DC, cascaded BJT common-emitter stages (devices) | 0.18 ms | 6.7 ms | 440 ms |
| Transient, RC ladder over 200 steps (stages) | 0.95 ms | 15 ms | 143 ms |

A 50 Hz half-wave rectifier with a filter cap over five cycles (5 000 steps) takes 9 ms. A transient session a microcontroller drives for 10 s, writing a pin and reading the filtered output every millisecond (10 000 updates, 130 000 steps at a 100 µs `tstep`), takes 73 ms. The cascaded BJT row grows faster than linearly, because each stage's bias depends on the one before it and Newton needs more iterations as the chain lengthens. `benches/mna_solve.rs` has the raw dense and sparse solve times up to 10 000 nodes (`--features internals`).

Pull requests run these benchmarks against their base on the same runner, and CI fails if any case is more than 25 % slower.

#### In the browser

The same solves built for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` (release) take 1.3–1.8× as long as native, on the same Apple M1 Pro:

| Case | Native | Chrome 157 | Ratio | Node 24 | Ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Operating point, 50 resistors and 50 diodes | 0.30 ms | 0.55 ms | 1.8× | 0.54 ms | 1.8× |
| Transient, the rectifier over 5 000 steps | 5.3 ms | 8.5 ms | 1.6× | 9.5 ms | 1.8× |
| AC, 100 RC stages at 100 frequencies | 5.1 ms | 6.4 ms | 1.3× | 6.4 ms | 1.3× |
| Transient session, a pin written every 1 ms for 10 s (130 000 steps) | 73 ms | — | — | 134 ms | 1.8× |

`sindr/tests/wasm_speed.rs` times them; its header has the commands for native, Node and a browser.

### Serde

With the default `serde` feature, `Circuit` and `SimulationResult` (and all nested types) implement `Serialize`/`Deserialize`. Component types use snake_case tags:

```json
{
  "ground_node": "0",
  "components": [
    { "type": "voltage_source", "id": "V1", "nodes": ["n1", "0"], "voltage": 10.0 },
    { "type": "resistor",       "id": "R1", "nodes": ["n1", "0"], "resistance": 1000.0 },
    { "type": "bjt",  "id": "Q1", "nodes": ["b", "c", "e"], "kind": "npn", "bf": 100 },
    { "type": "transformer", "id": "T1", "nodes": ["p1","q1","p2","q2"], "l1": 1e-3, "l2": 4e-3 },
    { "type": "varactor", "id": "D1", "nodes": ["a", "k"], "params": { "cj0": 10e-12, "phi": 0.7, "m": 0.5 } }
  ]
}
```
